steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Proscenium arch: audience on one side, framed stage — creates a 'fourth wall', common in traditional theatres.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Thrust stage: audience on three sides — intimate, breaks fourth wall, used in Shakespeare's Globe.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: In-the-round: audience on all sides — most intimate, actors must keep moving to avoid backs to audience.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Traverse: audience on two opposite sides — creates a catwalk/battle effect, highly dynamic.

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Name three stage types and explain how each affects the audience-performer relationship. | A director wants to create an intimate, immersive experience. Which stage type would you recommend and why? | Compare the advantages and disadvantages of performing in-the-round versus a proscenium arch stage.

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: Three named types with clear explanation of audience positioning and the performer relationship — e.g. proscenium creates distance/thrust creates intimacy/in-the-round creates total immersion. | A justified recommendation (e.g. promenade or in-the-round) with specific reasons about audience proximity, sight lines and the immersive qualities the stage type enables. | A balanced comparison: in-the-round gives intimacy and 360-degree audience engagement but requires constant movement management; proscenium allows controlled focus and set design but creates distance.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Always name the stage type precisely — never just say 'a normal stage' Link stage choice to the EFFECT on the audience Consider practical implications: sight lines, exits, set placement Use diagrams in your notes to remember configurations
